image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Composite election results graphic** consisting of:
  - a **stacked horizontal bar** showing electoral-vote totals at the top,
  - a **tile grid cartogram** of U.S. states in the middle,
  - a **choropleth-style U.S. map** at the bottom,
  - plus repeated **text summary labels** for candidates, vote counts, and percentages.

## 2) Layout techniques
- **Multiple panels / vertically stacked views**: the same election outcome is shown in separate panels.
- **Stacking**: the electoral-vote summary bar is stacked by candidate.
- **Tile grid layout**: the middle panel uses equal-sized tiles arranged geographically approximately by state.
- **Geographic map layout**: the bottom panel uses state shapes positioned geographically.
- **Color encoding** distinguishes candidate/winner.
- **Pattern/texture (hatching)** appears on some states to indicate a secondary status category (as shown in the legend: “Win” / “Flip”).

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Candidate name (Joseph R. Biden Jr., Donald J. Trump) | Categorical/nominal | Text labels; color of associated text/legend |
| Electoral votes | Quantitative | Length/position in stacked horizontal bar; large numeric labels (306, 232) |
| Popular vote count | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Popular vote percentage | Quantitative | Text labels beneath candidate names |
| Winning threshold (“270 TO WIN”) | Quantitative | Reference marker/label on stacked bar |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual tile/map region; state abbreviation labels |
| State winner / candidate | Categorical/nominal | Fill color of tiles and map regions (blue/red) |
| State status (Win vs Flip, per legend) | Categorical/nominal | Hatching/texture over state tiles and map regions |
| Maine/Nebraska electoral-vote district split units (e.g., Maine 1, Maine 2, Neb. 1, Neb. 2, Neb. 3) | Categorical/nominal | Separate legend entries and separate colored map units |

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I noticed were the flipped states; I noticed that Biden flipped AZ, PA, GA, MI, WI, and a district in NE. The second thing I noticed was the main difference between the 2  maps; the 1st map breaks the states down by the number of electoral votes while the 2nd map shows states, their geographical borders, and how the state voted as a whole. The setup of the 2nd map is a bit misleading. For example, in Nebraska, Trump won the state, but Biden won the 2nd congressional district and 1 out of 5 of Nebraska's electoral college votes. An individual wouldn't be able to gather that information from the second map and would have a false sense of complete unity within each state. Whereas the 1st map highlights the disunity and conflicting views within states. I wonder which map is more commonly published and why. This has a large impact on me personally; I am a senior in high school, so the stance of the party in the White House holds on student loans will have a large impact on my financial situation throughout college and the beginning of my adult life. My community will also feel the impacts of this decision -- both beneficial and harmful. I live in a rural community that has a lack of access to adequate healthcare and the new administration's policy aims to improve that, but my community is also comprised of a majority of farmers, who were greatly dependant upon the subsidies under the Trump administration. Catchy Headline: Is America Red, Blue, or Purple?

comments.raw_comment: I notice that both maps display the 2020 election results, but the first map does so more accurately. In the first map, each state is depicted by the number of electoral votes, one block representing one vote. The second map shows the states’ actual sizes which are colored to represent whoever won that state. In the second map, it falsely suggests that bigger states carry more weight in the election which is why Trump appears to be leading. By completely ignoring the electoral vote, it does not consider the weight each states’ votes have accounting for their population, as the first map does. Oklahoma is much larger than Connecticut on the second map when in reality, they have the same amount of electoral votes. I wonder why the second map is what we most commonly see during elections? It can be very misleading as it does not account for smaller states with higher populations, which in this case are the majority of what Biden won. I also wonder why Nebraska and Maine have split electoral votes? I’m curious what the advantage is of doing this is instead of using winner takes all like every other state. This has an impact on my community and me because New Hampshire is a geographically small state. The first map reveals that our votes may be weighted more than we realize, every vote does count. NH has only one less electoral vote than Colorado, which appears much larger on the second map. My headline is: “Are the Maps We Usually See as Accurate as We’ve Been Led To Believe?"

Noticed: These maps show how, overall, there are certain trends of voting depending on where you live.  If you live in more rural areas, then you will likely vote republican, and if you live in urban areas, then you will likely vote democrat.  I also think that Wis., Arz., Ga., Pa., and Mich. are all states that were fought over intensely, as they all flipped their votes.  I think it is interesting that there are no red flipped states, potentially showing how the Republican party was dominant in such areas.

Wonder:
I wonder what would happen if you changed the electoral votes to based on the size of the state. I think that it would be interesting because it would be different. I also think that if the states were judged based on size, Trump would have won because he has the rural places. I wonder what the maps would look like if fewer states had the winner take all rule. I also wonder how much the results would change. 


Impacts: 
What impact does this have on you and your community?
I think that this will affect my community by putting a lot of stress on my family and friends. This would put stress on my peeps because this matters a lot and will affect us for the next four years.

The first graph shows the number of electoral votes per state and whether each individual vote was a win or was flipped. I wonder how the environment, culture, and lifestyle of each state affects the views of voters and the candidate that they end up voting for. In addition, many people don't fully understand the Electoral College and how votes are secured. Massachusetts is known to be a democratic and blue state, so it's interesting to see how other states fall in the political spectrum. 

A headline could be "Breaking Down the Election: Understanding the Electoral College."

-What do you notice?:
In the second graph, without any prior knowledge as to how U.S elections work, it would appear as though Donald Trump won. We on the other hand, know that this is not the case and although there are more red states than blue, with the understanding of the electoral college we can deduce that Joe Biden was the winner. I also notice how the first graph is broken down into electoral college votes from each state, making it clearer and easier to see how it is that Joe Biden won this election.
   -What do you wonder?:
One of the main wonderings I have about these graphs, and the way U.S elections are run in the first place, is why certain states have long standing histories of voting for a certain party, while there are others we classify as ‘swing states’. What is it that causes these distinctions to happen and why are they so consistent?
   -What impact does this have on you and your community?:
I feel as though the impact this has on me and my community is more widespread than meets the eye. If every U.S citizen a look at some of the proven information about the election I believe that there would be less conflict and argument over what is factual information and what is “fake news” per se. 
   -Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea:
“A Deeper Look into the 2020 Presidential Election Maps”

For instance, when I was talking to one of my friends about the election, they said that if there wasn't a bar on the top of the map showing who was winning, they would think that the Republican was winning, although, in reality, it's the Democrat. A heading for the top map could be "Election Results by Electoral Vote", and a heading for the bottom map could be "Election Results by States' Popular Vote". In conclusion, I feel that the top map gives people a better idea of not only how the electoral college works, but who is truly winning the election, and why, even though the Republican had more states' popular vote, the Democrat actually was winning.

Keep noticing and wondering.  The next release will be by Friday, Dec. 4 with moderation on Wednesday, Dec. 9.  The graph is about how the United States compares to countries worldwide.

4. These graphs show the 2020 election in two different ways, electoral votes, and which party won the state, the second way more misleading.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I notice from these maps is how the change in how the data is displayed makes a big difference in interpreting the data. In the top map, the states are represented based on their electoral votes, making it appear that Biden received more votes, which is accurate. In the bottom map, states are colored by which candidate won them overall, making it appear as if Trump won more of the country. This is misleading because the areas that Trump won are less populated than where Biden won, leading to Biden's win. I wonder how people working in the polling industry use the displaying of data to guide the population to one belief or another. I find it interesting but worrying that people who make political maps can use the human eye to make people believe something that isn’t true. This is the impact that these maps have on my community: we all see things every day that are misleading, but we often believe these things anyway. I hope that non-misleading forms of visual data will become more widely used so that data presented to the public does not come with forms of bias. In terms of what is going on in each map, they both represent two very different things. For the top map, I would title this one “Which Candidate Won the Majority of Electoral Votes?." I would title the bottom map “The 2020 Presidential Candidate That Won Each State,” as this map does not break the states down into a respective size based on the number of electoral votes.

I notice that the first graph is visualized using blocks. The number of blocks for each state represents the number of electoral votes. I wonder why the second map that shows each state by majority vote is used more when the first map that shows the electoral votes is the most important?

Overall, both graphs show the importance of everyone voting.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that the first map shows sizes the states in proportion to how many electoral votes they have, with each cube representing one vote. There is clearly more blue shown than red, which aligns with the actual result of the election. The second graph, on the other hand, simply shows each state as it appears normally on a map. Here there is a higher volume of red than blue, contrary to the election results. 
I wonder whether the second map has misled people into thinking the election was closer than it is, or if it caused people to make the argument of “more land is red, so Trump should have won.” I also wonder why maps like the first one, which accurately display the voting power of each state, are rarely used even though they convey the data more accurately.
The difference between these two graphs truly shows me and my community how the physical size of a state doesn’t matter when it comes to electoral power. As someone from New Hampshire, it’s fascinating to look at the first map and see our tiny state portrayed as bigger than Alaska, the largest state in the US.
These graphs show the disparity between land size and electoral votes, as well as the voter demographics across our country. Just by looking at them we can infer that people living in areas of high population density such as cities tend to vote Democrat, while those living in more rural areas tend to vote Republican. An idea for a headline would be “Land Doesn’t Vote, People Do.”

comments.raw_comment:
1. I notice that the first graph shows each state as a group of boxes. Each box represents one of the states’ electoral votes. This allows the viewer to understand how much influence each state has on the election because every states’ size is determined by the number of electoral votes it has. The second graph  shows the geographical area of each state, which makes it difficult to discern how much impact each state has on the election.

2. I wonder why the most common graph used by news outlets to reflect election results is the graph that shows the geographical size of each state. These graphs can cause confusion because they are usually mostly red, giving the impression that the republican candidate won the election even when they did not. This is because they fail to show that although there are fewer blue states, many have larger populations and more electoral votes than republican states. Graphs that show each states’ number of electoral votes clearly convey this information, so they should be used instead.

3. These graphs show what areas voted for which candidate, which helps us determine if we are living in a generally liberal or conservative area. For example, I can understand from this graph that I live in a generally liberal region of the United States because the state I live in and many of the surrounding states are blue.

4. Both of these graphs reflect the 2020 election results by showing which candidate won each state.

A Tale of Two Graphs

After observing both graphs, I noticed the effect the two colors had on my eyes. The red coloring was deceiving, especially in the second graph. When I observed the first graph, I had an easier time identifying that blue had the majority of the votes. I could look at each state and tell that there were more blue states than red states. Having the states separated and not touching was a major help when identifying the winner. When I looked at the second graph, the red color stood out. It looked as if red held the majority of the votes. 
I wonder why the red coloring has this effect on my eyes. I did not have a problem observing the first graph but I did with the second. All the red seemed to blend together and looked as if it was the majority. 
If other observers share the same issues I had while reading the second graph, my community including me could easily confuse the winner of the 2020 election. Reading a graph incorrectly can cause a negative impact throughout a community. People may look at the second graph as I did and confuse the winners. A community could become very confused and separated over a graph like the second one. It gives the correct results but presents them in a misleading way. One person may read the graph correctly and one person may not. This could cause a feud between these two people or even a whole community. 
A new headline that captures the maps’ main idea is the deceiving red.

comments.raw_comment:
When analyzing the two displays, I noticed several different things.  The most prominent is that the graphs attempt to portray different things.  The first values data over looks, specifically, it shows the number of electoral votes for each state instead of the correct shape and cleanliness of the state.  The second graph takes a more traditional approach, and shades states in with whichever color it sided with.  I’m interested in the first graph since it takes an unorthodox approach to presenting the information.  
Since electoral votes are based on the population of a state, I wonder if each vote is directly proportional to a percentage of the state.  For example, if one of New Hampshire’s votes represents more or less people than say for one of California’s votes.  
Since we live in a relatively small state with a low population, I’m not surprised with our electoral college votes compared to our state size.  It appears that we are on the lower end of states when considering electoral college votes, but that isn’t necessarily a bad thing.
Since the first graph appears to present data more accurately, I would question the authenticity or effectiveness of the second graph in a title comparing the two.  A catchy title that I came up with could be “Has looking simple ruined our perception of an efficient display of information?”

Both of these states vote blue by a longshot and are both coastal states. States like Washington, Oregon, and New Jersey are also densely populated areas on coastal areas that tend to vote blue. However, two states with large populations, Texas and Florida voted red this election. What I found interesting was that the democrats were able to win states like Wisconsin, Michigan, and Georgia which were previously red. This made me wonder why these states went blue this election, whether COVID played a role, and what the democrats did that the republicans did not.

2.) What are some policies that encapsulate densely populated areas and shift these communities to vote blue?  The Midwest does not nearly make as much of the population up as these cities, yet makes 2/3 of the land and tends to be mostly red. Where does this polarization between densely populated and rural areas spur from?

3.) Josh Gottheimer, who is my congressman, has a history of working across the aisle to ensure that people get necessary social programs but the economic stability of the region remains unaffected. I am not surprised by these election results and I believe that life goes on.

4.) A Tale of Two Backgrounds: The Increasing Polarization of Rural and Urban Areas

1. I noticed that most of the states that we would normally consider "republican" Trump was able to win (those in the mid-West and South). But, on the Electoral College votes winner-map, we are able to see the distribution of votes is not always overwhelmingly for one candidate. We are able to see in Nebraska and Maine there is one small box in the state that actually went the other way (in Nebraska it went blue, in Maine it went red). This displays clearly the idea of winner-takes-all in most American states, outside of the very few exceptions like Nebraska and Maine, who stand out for not having just one color or another.
2. I wonder if it is likely that the first map could be used more often if the Electoral System was either abolished or strongly reformed. Each state would then have a chance to have different winners per "block" in their state, possibly giving way to more diverse opinions and a more fair system of voting in president. I also wonder why states in the mid-West so strongly associate with Trump, even though many of Trump's policies hurt working-class men and women. In many of these states, the very people voting for Trump are most likely negatively affected by his politics. 
3. Once again, Ohio went red during this election. Ohio is considered a swing-state, meaning that the results in our state and my community is very important to the presidential race. Voting in my community and state is therefore very important.
4. "Winner Takes All: Biden Wins"

The first map shows a more accurate representation of the results, as a glance at the second map shows an overwhelming amount of red.

In regards to the coronavirus, Biden’s victory signifies an upcoming change to our country’s pandemic response. Since my community is a traditionally blue area, we will most likely adopt Biden’s new ideas, whether that means mandatory vaccinations or a mask mandate.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that the two graphical displays highlight how bias and misleading appearances are used in politics. In the first graph, the voting results are shown in accordance to the state population, whereas, in the second graph, the results are shown with colors according to the proportion of the state land. The second graph holds more bias in favor of the republican party because, at first glance ,it looks like there are more red voters due to the fact that the states who voted red are larger. However, as the first graph displays, the population is denser in the states that voted blue, which explains why the democratic candidate won. One specific example of the difference in graphical displays is the difference in sizes in states such as New York, being physically smaller state in reference to land area, but was displayed bigger in the first graph because of its large population.
